snip.t: Bilaterality is a frequent characteristic of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS).
Clonal expansion of mutated bronchial epithelial cells → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma
Highest risk: lobular carcinoma in situ (about 8 to 10 times).

Zoon's (plasma cell) balanitis: a well-defined red, flat lesion with "cayenne pepper" spots on the glans or prepuce in older uncircumcised men (resembles carcinoma in situ, so biopsy); circumcision treats it.
snip.s: Penile Conditions: Benign Lesions, Premalignant Disease and Penile Cancer

snip.t: Erythroplasia of Queyrat (squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the glans and prepuce, non-keratinising): velvety bright red plaques; almost only in uncircumcised men; progression to invasive cancer in 10 to 33%.
snip.s: Penile Conditions: Benign Lesions, Premalignant Disease and Penile Cancer

snip.t: Risk factors: cryptorchidism (3 to 8 times; the risk persists after orchidopexy), a family history (father or brother), a previous testicular cancer (contralateral), infertility, HIV, hypospadias, carcinoma in situ, in-utero exposure (DES), and Klinefelter's syndrome.

qs.q: A 70‑year‑old man is found to have high‑grade T1 urothelial carcinoma with concomitant carcinoma in situ on pathology after transurethral resection. He is considered at the highest risk for disease progression. Which definitive surgical approach is recommended for this patient?
qs.e: Radical cystectomy provides the most reliable cure for highest‑risk non‑muscle‑invasive disease because it removes the entire bladder and potential sites of invasion. Partial cystectomy does not address the diffuse CIS component and thus is insufficient.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer: Haematuria, TURBT, BCG and Cystectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a well-defined red, flat lesion with characteristic 'cayenne pepper' spots on his glans. A skin biopsy is performed to rule out carcinoma in situ, confirming Zoon's plasma cell balanitis. What is the definitive treatment for this condition?
qs.e: Zoon's plasma cell balanitis occurs in older uncircumcised men and is definitively treated by circumcision, which eliminates the moist preputial environment maintaining the inflammation. Topical steroids only offer temporary relief.
qs.s: Penile Conditions: Benign Lesions, Premalignant Disease and Penile: MCQs

qs.q: A 55-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a velvety bright red plaque strictly confined to the glans penis. Histology reveals non-keratinising squamous cell carcinoma in situ. What is the most accurate classification of this premalignant lesion?
qs.e: Erythroplasia of Queyrat is squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the glans and prepuce presenting as velvety bright red plaques almost exclusively in uncircumcised men. Bowen's disease typically affects the penile shaft with keratinising lesions.
qs.s: Penile Conditions: Benign Lesions, Premalignant Disease and Penile: MCQs

qs.q: A 45‑year‑old man is diagnosed with erythroplasia of Queyrat confined to the prepuce. After confirming carcinoma in situ on biopsy, which treatment is most likely sufficient?
qs.e: Circumcision removes the affected prepuce and can be curative when the lesion is limited. Wide excision or Mohs are more extensive than needed for isolated preputial disease.
qs.s: Penile Conditions: Benign Lesions, Premalignant Disease and Penile: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following treatments for penile carcinoma in situ is associated with the highest recurrence rate?
qs.e: Cryotherapy has a higher recurrence rate compared with other modalities. The other options provide more controlled tissue destruction.
qs.s: Penile Conditions: Benign Lesions, Premalignant Disease and Penile: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate primary treatment for Bowen’s disease (penile carcinoma in situ)?
qs.e: Total penectomy is excessive for a lesion confined to the epithelium. The other options are organ‑preserving modalities suitable for in situ disease.
qs.s: Penile Conditions: Benign Lesions, Premalignant Disease and Penile: MCQs

qs.q: Why is Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) frequently detected on routine screening mammograms?
o: Central cell death leads to visible calcifications
The cancer cells lose E-cadherin and form aggregates
It causes immediate skin dimpling and retraction
qs.e: DCIS is found on mammograms because cells in the centre of the ducts die and calcify, producing visible calcifications. LCIS, by contrast, does not cause calcifications and is invisible on imaging.
qs.s: Breast Carcinoma: Understanding Types, Receptors & Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: What specific microscopic architecture defines the cribriform pattern of Ductal Carcinoma In Situ?
o: Central parts of the duct dying and becoming necrotic
True fibrovascular cores forming branching fronds
Cells forming round cookie-cutter spaces in ducts
Small finger-like projections without a blood vessel
qs.e: The cribriform pattern of DCIS is characterized by cells forming round cookie-cutter like spaces inside the duct. Comedo pattern features central necrosis, whereas micropapillary lacks a central blood vessel.
qs.s: Breast Carcinoma: Understanding Types, Receptors & Treatment: MCQs
